task.description: CODE-DESIGNER (WF-02 Step 1) for REQ-162: design how uncaught Lua runtime errors are captured host-side and converted into a structured SCRIPT_ERROR value (LUA-16 restated). Read docs/requirements.yaml's REQ-162 entry in full before designing anything -- the queue task's full description, restatement reasoning, and 8 real acceptance criteria are there verbatim. Read lib/letflow/design/req148-lua-runtime-spike.md Section 5 (OQ-2 (c)) FIRST: it already empirically found the consumed-instruction count IS retrievable, via `lua_after.state.instruction_count` (an internal, undocumented Lua.VM.State struct field, not a formal public API -- the spike itself says 'S5 requirements that read it must document the mechanism explicitly and include a regression test so a future library upgrade that removes or renames the field fails loudly'). Cite this by section, do not re-run the spike. However, the spike's experiment measured instruction_count after a NORMAL, successful Lua.eval!/2 return -- this design must independently determine (by reading the real deps/lua source, the same rigor REQ-159/160/161's designs applied) whether that same state/field is still reachable at the point an UNCAUGHT runtime error propagates out of Lua.eval!/2 as a raised Lua.RuntimeException, since REQ-162's own scope is specifically the uncaught-error path, not the successful-completion path the spike measured. Read deps/lua/lib/lua.ex's rescue/reraise clauses (lines ~556-605) directly to determine this -- do not assume the spike's successful-path finding transfers unchanged to the error path. If the count is genuinely unreachable on the error path (even though reachable on success), REQ-162's own restatement text requires branch (b): drop the field or report the configured budget instead, and say so explicitly -- never zero-fill or omit-but-imply-present. Read lib/letflow/engine/lua/executor.ex in full: REQ-153/154/155/156 already own the Lua.eval!/2 call boundary and its various kill/timeout/budget mechanisms -- REQ-162's error capture most likely lives here (in the existing rescue/catch structure around Lua.eval!/2), not in platform.ex, since platform.ex's host functions are called FROM inside Lua.eval!/2, not the site that observes an error escaping it. Read lib/letflow/design/req161-lua-platform-fail.md's section 3.3/4 (SCRIPT_FAILED's own shape and the executor.ex stringification gap) to keep SCRIPT_ERROR and SCRIPT_FAILED reserved-tag-disjoint and consistent with that design's own reservation. Read lib/letflow/engine/lua/capabilities.ex for the real capability-set type this design must read from (not re-derive) for the 'capability state at failure' field. Design the SCRIPT_ERROR shape so it is pattern-match-distinguishable from all 4 other arms this codebase already produces at the same boundary: REQ-161's {:script_failed, _}, REQ-154's instruction-budget error, REQ-155's wall-clock timeout, REQ-156's memory-limit error -- read each of those 4 real shapes directly in executor.ex, do not assume their shape from memory. Also determine, empirically by reading deps/lua's real Lua 5.3 semantics (or by reasoning from the vendored VM source, mirroring REQ-161's design's own deps/lua-reading rigor) which division form (1//0, 1%0, or another) actually raises in this runtime, since 1/0 yields inf and does not raise -- LUA-16's literal 'division by zero' acceptance criterion is a Lua 5.1 assumption that does not fire as written. Design a stack-trace sanitization approach that strips host filesystem paths and Elixir module internals a script author does not need (SECURITY-REVIEWER hard gate -- this is a data-disclosure surface). Write the design to lib/letflow/design/req162-lua-script-error-capture.md and a prose test spec skeleton to test/specs/REQ-162.md. Zero literal Elixir code in the design doc -- @spec/@type signatures only, everything else prose/tables.
acceptance_criteria: Design cites REQ-148 spike Section 5 (OQ-2 (c)) by section for the successful-path instruction_count finding, and independently determines (via direct deps/lua source reading) whether that field is still reachable on the UNCAUGHT-ERROR path specifically -- not merely assumed to transfer.

Design states explicitly which restatement branch holds (instruction count retrievable on the error path, or not) and, if not, what is reported instead (never a zero-filled or silently-omitted field passed off as a measurement).

Design specifies exactly where SCRIPT_ERROR capture happens (most likely executor.ex's existing Lua.eval!/2 call boundary, not platform.ex) and why, based on a direct reading of executor.ex's current rescue/catch structure.

Design specifies the SCRIPT_ERROR value's exact shape, and a traceability argument (backed by reading the real code) that it is pattern-match-distinguishable from all 4 other real arms this codebase already produces: SCRIPT_FAILED (REQ-161), instruction-budget error (REQ-154), wall-clock timeout (REQ-155), memory-limit error (REQ-156).
Design specifies that capability state at failure is read from REQ-157's real capability-set type (lib/letflow/engine/lua/capabilities.ex), not re-derived or reconstructed.

Design identifies which Lua 5.3 division form (1//0, 1%0, or other) actually raises in the adopted runtime, substituting it for the literal 'division by zero' acceptance text, and documents why the substitution is necessary.
Design specifies a stack-trace sanitization mechanism that a SECURITY-REVIEWER can verify strips host filesystem paths and Elixir module internals not needed by a script author.
All 8 real acceptance criteria from docs/requirements.yaml's REQ-162 entry mapped to concrete design elements in a traceability table.
Zero literal Elixir code anywhere in the design doc -- @spec/@type only.
